inline.s: The supreme, foremost, rarest Dharma — what Dharma is it? It is none other than the Dharma of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, the Dharma of the ultimate enlightenment known by self-verification. To accomplish this Dharma is precisely what is meant by becoming a Buddha. The Amitābha Sutra says that Śākyamuni is able to accomplish the most difficult and rarest of things, able amid the five turbidities and evil ages to attain anuttarā-bodhi. “Most difficult and rarest” is the rarest of the rare. Nothing stands above a Buddha, hence “supreme.” If we parse the words: anuttarā-bodhi means supreme, perfect, and universal enlightenment. “Perfect enlightenment” — from beginningless time one was unawakened, and now one can turn from dust and unite with enlightenment: is this not rare? “Universal” — universal means equal. Now one is not only self-enlightened but can enlighten others; self and other are non-dual, emptiness and existence are both ungrasped, and this equal dharma-realm is the supreme meaning: hence “foremost.” “Supreme” — to reach the treasury of jewels directly and realize the ultimate enlightenment, which is called supreme bodhi. “Supreme” is the very meaning of “foremost.” The old commentaries were vague and terse; here I state it precisely so that its meaning may be known. As for the explanations given by later writers, some expound it by the three bodies, some by the three kinds of prajñā; such meanings are less intimate and complete. “Accomplish” means that there is the possibility of accomplishing this Dharma. “Such a person” refers generally to anyone who, wherever this sutra is spoken, can fully receive and uphold it, and to anyone who, hearing the sutra, can receive and uphold it and can speak of it accordingly. The words “you should know” govern all that follows. Taken in this sentence alone, they mean that such a person cultivates both merit and wisdom, saves both self and others, and so will head straight for the treasury of jewels and attain great accomplishment — such a one must not be slighted. If you know that this person accomplishes the inconceivable, you know that their merit far surpasses that of one who gives the seven treasures filling boundless and limitless great chiliocosms. One is defiled and conditioned; the other is undefiled and unconditioned. Here lies the whole difference — what is there to wonder at?
(Yin) Second, concluding in terms of permeation.
“Wherever this sutra is found, there is the Buddha, and there are venerable disciples.”

In Chinese the character jing, “sutra,” originally carries the sense of a path; dian, “canon,” carries the sense of a standard. What this sutra sets forth is in every case the unchanging true path for those who have aroused the bodhi mind, the road of awakening held in common. To walk this road and follow this standard is naturally to arrive straight at the treasury of jewels. Therefore wherever this sutra is, that place is the treasury of jewels. Since it is the treasury of jewels, the Buddha and all the worthies and sages are never absent from it. “And there are venerable disciples” is another way of saying “and all the worthies and sages.” Ruo, “and,” means “as well as.” “Venerable disciples,” some say, refers to Kāśyapa, Maudgalyāyana, and the great disciples; some say it refers to Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the great bodhisattvas. In sum, wherever the Buddha is, there is an assembly gathered around him to hear the Dharma, as the stars surround the moon. So “venerable disciples” is a general term covering all worthies and sages, bodhisattvas, and arhats, without needing to single any out. The Great Prajñā Sutra says: wherever prajñā is, the Buddhas of the ten directions are always within it. Therefore one who wishes to make offerings to the Buddha should know to make offerings to prajñā. Prajñā and the Buddha are not two, not different. Knowing that the Buddhas of the ten directions are all here, one knows that all bodhisattvas and arhats throughout the whole of space and the entire dharma-realm are all here as well. All of this is simply to make clear that this sutra is supremely excellent: wherever it is, the place is honored; in whomever it is, the person is honored.

Surveying the several sections above: first the place where the sutra is spoken was set forth, then the person who receives and upholds it. By this point we know that setting forth the place and the person was in truth to set forth the merit of this sutra. That merit is nothing other than the right wisdom of prajñā. So setting forth the sutra is in turn truly to urge people to make offerings to this sutra, to read and recite it, to receive and uphold it, and to explain it widely to others, in the hope that through words they may give rise to contemplation and realize true reality. Such is the Buddha’s way of teaching the Dharma: its glance falls in all four directions, and every side is complete.

Again, when the place was first set forth, it was said that one should make offerings to it as to a Buddha’s stūpa or temple: this declares that the sutra itself is the dwelling Three Jewels. Now it is said that wherever the sutra is, there is the Buddha and all the worthies and sages: this declares the permanently abiding Three Jewels. And in between it is said that such a person accomplishes the supreme, foremost, rarest Dharma: this declares that they accomplish the Three Jewels of self-nature. Put together, this means that through the dwelling Three Jewels one realizes the Three Jewels of self-nature and accomplishes the permanently abiding Three Jewels; that is, because it abides permanently it dwells, and because it dwells it abides permanently. And how does it dwell, how does it abide permanently? It depends entirely on self-nature to accomplish this.

Again, above the accomplishment was called supreme in order to show the reason for the supremacy of the merit. Now permeation is called supreme in order to show the reason for the supremacy of the accomplishment. Why so? Because where the sutra is, there are the Buddhas and bodhisattvas. One who upholds and teaches it is therefore drawing near to the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and all the great spiritual friends. Permeating one’s own nature thus at every moment, how could one fail to attain great accomplishment?

Again, it was first said that the place is “as a Buddha’s stūpa or temple.” How is the place where the sutra is spoken like a Buddha’s stūpa or temple? Now it is said that wherever the sutra is, the Buddha and the worthies and sages are all present — is this not making plain the reason for the earlier words, “as a Buddha’s stūpa or temple”? In sum, to say “as a Buddha’s stūpa or temple” and then to say “the Buddha and the worthies and sages are all present” both make clear that this sutra is bound up with the very lifeblood of the Three Jewels. Hence the Buddha did not shrink from speaking in detail, over and over, to make all living beings honor this sutra.

Again, having spoken of accomplishment above, the Buddha immediately continues that wherever the sutra is, there is the Buddha, and there are venerable disciples. This further makes plain that the accomplishment of such a person is, at the highest, like the Buddha’s, and at the next level, like that of all the worthies and sages, and is the rarest of the rare. Why so? One who arouses the mind that dwells nowhere should realize the unconditioned fruit; hence all worthies and sages are distinguished by the unconditioned Dharma. So one who upholds and teaches this sutra of the unconditioned, true reality — how could such a one fail to accomplish this Dharma?

These several sections of sutra text contain few words but inexhaustible wondrous meaning; it can never be fully expounded. Here I have only touched on it lightly, as set out above. It remains for each person to grasp it well.

Again, in the earlier comparison the merit of the sutra was shown by comparing it with the gift of the treasures of one great chiliocosm. Now it is shown by comparing it with the gift of the treasures of boundless and limitless great chiliocosms. Why is there such a difference between the earlier and the later? What does it mean? The earlier showing of supremacy came after the teaching on being able to give rise to faith, and it said that all Buddhas and the supreme, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas issue from this sutra. This makes clear that if one can hear these chapters and verses and one’s faith becomes pure, one is already tending toward Buddha-wisdom, and so has such merit. But that was only the initial arising of pure faith, not yet deep; hence supremacy was shown only by the gift of the treasures of one great chiliocosm. Now it is otherwise: this is said after the opening of understanding. What is the opening of understanding? It is what is called giving rise to a pure mind, giving rise to the mind that dwells nowhere. And it says that you should know such a person accomplishes the supreme, foremost, rarest Dharma, and further that there is the Buddha and there are venerable disciples. This makes clear that if one can comprehend the true meaning of dwelling nowhere while giving rise to the mind and giving rise to the mind while dwelling nowhere, there is the possibility of great, great accomplishment. For by understanding the sutra’s meaning one gains its essential points. Compared with the earlier state of merely having faith but not yet the essential points, the distance is as heaven from earth. Therefore the gift of the treasures of boundless and limitless great chiliocosms is used in comparison to show supremacy. This makes clear that such a person’s merit exceeds that of the former by boundless and limitless times. Why so? The one has only just aroused faith and knows the words but roughly; the other deeply understands the sutra’s meaning and can gradually enter contemplation. You should know that this sutra is devoted to making plain true reality and pointing directly at the original mind. If one who receives and upholds it can truly take it up directly and, relying on the sutra, give rise to contemplation, then one generates merit, eradicates offenses, and swiftly realizes bodhi — how can such merit be measured! And as for the five comparisons in the first half of the sutra, if the sutra’s merit seems to be greater or lesser, it is in fact because the practice of those who recite and uphold it is shallow or deep that such differences arise; the merit of the sutra itself does not differ.

blocks.text: Section Thirteen: Receiving and Upholding in Accordance with the Dharma

inline.s: (Xin) Third, requesting instruction on the name and on upholding. This has two parts: (Ren) first, the request; next, the instruction.
(Ren) First, the request.
Then Subhūti said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what name should be given to this sutra? How should we receive and uphold it?”

The text that follows is subtle in meaning throughout, and you should listen attentively. Because the words interlock with what comes before and after, one must take the whole, before and after, and read them together, mutually illuminating each other, before the meaning becomes thorough. Since it is spoken as a synthesis of before and after, the meanings are dense and intricate. Heard in a daze, it is hard to grasp.

“Then” is the moment when what preceded has just ended. It implies that when the essential points have been grasped, one should at once put them into practice, without the slightest slackening. This is what is meant by “the moment of understanding is the moment of practice.” The compilers of the sutra deliberately marked “Then”; their intent lies here.

Again, wherever this sutra marks the phrase “Then Subhūti said to the Buddha,” it always indicates a fresh start — what is commonly called beginning a new paragraph — to show that what this section teaches advances beyond what came before, and to draw the reader’s attention. Yet although the words begin afresh, the meaning still follows on what preceded. For above, again and again, the supreme merit of this sutra was shown, to the point that wherever the sutra is, the Buddha and the worthies and sages are present with it. Such is its excellence. Can one fail to know its name? Again and again it was said that to receive and uphold this sutra, even a four-line verse of it, brings the greatest merit, and that to receive and uphold it fully accomplishes the Dharma of supreme bodhi. How then should one uphold it? These are matters that every student urgently needs to know. Hence the question: what name should be given to this sutra, and how should we receive and uphold it?

In other sutras, when the name of the sutra is asked, it is mostly given at the very end of the whole. Here alone it is given in the middle. Why? You should know that the meaning of the latter half of this sutra opens out from the former half; that meaning is already present in the former half, only it was not yet explained in detail. Had the elder not asked again, then once the former half was spoken the sutra could have come to an end. For this reason, although the name of this sutra appears to be given in the middle, it is in fact given at the end of the former half, and so is no different from other sutras.

“What name should be given to this sutra?” means: by what name should this sutra be named? The sentence may also be inverted: what name should this sutra have? Since its meaning is supreme, its name must be supreme as well. The implication is that the name must match the reality, and that knowing the name one may better understand the meaning from the name. “Receive” means to comply with and follow. “Uphold” means to cultivate and practice, to put into practice. The Buddha is asked to instruct in the method of upholding so that the great assembly may follow it; hence “how should we receive and uphold it?” “Receive and uphold” is much the same as “receive and practice.” Whenever practice is spoken of, two meanings are included: (1) practicing oneself; (2) urging others to practice. Hence the ancients explained the character chi, “to uphold,” as ren-hong, “to bear and to spread.” Ren, to bear, refers to practicing oneself; hong, to spread, refers to urging others to practice. To speak of putting into practice brings in everything said above. Consider: from the detailed talk onward, the Buddha opened by saying that one should subdue one’s mind. How does one subdue it? It is to arouse the great vow, practice the great practice, not dwell in the realm of the six dusts, practice the six pāramitās far and wide, save boundless living beings and bring them to Buddhahood, and yet not grasp the mark of saving living beings — and further, neither dharmas nor non-dharmas should be grasped. Peeling away layer after layer, ever more finely, it all comes down to not dwelling in the six dusts and giving rise to a pure mind. (These eight characters are an abbreviation of “one should give rise to a pure mind” and “not dwelling in the six dusts, give rise to the mind”; they are also a gloss on “one should give rise to the mind that dwells nowhere.”) All the various gateways of meaning taught here are gateways of contemplation and gateways of practice; that is, all are to be received and upheld. If so, the World-Honored One’s instruction to the assembly on how to receive and uphold was already utterly detailed and clear — why then did the elder Subhūti ask again here how to receive and uphold? Were all the meanings taught above meant only for comprehension, not for upholding? Or is there something not yet exhausted in upholding what was taught above, so that he now asks again? It is precisely here that the earlier remark applies: one must take the whole, before and after, and read it as a synthesis. If such points are not thoroughly understood, one’s upholding will lack power, and one will not merely fall into the misunderstandings described above. You should know that the elder’s present question, “how should we receive and uphold it?,” carries a deeper intent.

(1) Whatever the Buddha teaches is always perfect in principle and in practice. “Perfect” means that when principle is taught, practice is included; when practice is taught, principle is included. This is what is meant by “outside principle there is no practice, outside practice there is no principle.” Hence a student of Buddhism must advance in understanding and practice together. Understanding belongs to the side of principle, practice to the side of practice; only by advancing in both does one accord with perfection. But the capacities of living beings differ in a thousand ways. There are naturally those who understand and practice at once; there are also those who understand but cannot yet practice, or who practice but cannot yet accord. You should know that to understand without practicing, or to practice without according, is in truth not to have understood. One who can truly comprehend will practice without waiting to be urged, and the practice will accord of itself. The elder wished to give such people one further step of understanding, and so asked again: this is what is meant by an overly earnest, grandmotherly heart.

(2) To ask the name of the sutra is to request instruction on the overall title of all the words, chapters, and verses spoken above. To ask how to receive and uphold it is likewise to request instruction on whether all the meanings taught above have a method of total retention. If one gains the total retention and holds this overall title, is that not all the more essential? This is what is meant by never tiring of hearing the Dharma. If you grasp the first layer of principle here, you will know that although the Buddha was not asked above how to receive and uphold, he was not solely teaching comprehension — upholding was already included. And now, although upholding is asked about, the wish for yet further understanding is still included as well. If you grasp the second layer, you will know that since there was upholding before, there is no harm in asking again now. Thus the earlier and the later not only do not conflict or repeat, but can further bring out the earlier meaning.

Having come this far, lest people give rise to further doubt, I must now speak once more, thoroughly. Question: since everything taught above should be received and upheld, and now the sutra plainly asks how to receive and uphold, why is the first great section judged to be about generating faith, the second great section about opening understanding, and only the third great section about progressive cultivation? (In the detailed exposition, there are first two overall sections: first, clarifying non-dwelling in terms of objects; next, clarifying non-dwelling in terms of mind. These two overall sections are then divided into four: 1. generating faith, 2. opening understanding, 3. progressive cultivation, 4. accomplishing realization.) Answer: from the opening of the sutra onward, cultivation is in fact possible throughout; but the ultimate method of cultivation lies in the third great section. Hence only the third great section is given the name “progressive cultivation.” Moreover, this follows the sutra itself; it is not presumptuous invention. In the first great section it is plainly pointed out that observing the precepts and cultivating merit can generate faith: this makes clear the first arising of faith. Hence it is judged to be about generating faith. In the second great section, after the request for instruction on the name and on upholding, deep understanding of the meaning is pointed out: this makes clear that not only has faith arisen, understanding has been opened. Hence it is judged to be about opening understanding. And as the third great section nears its end, it plainly points out that by cultivating all good dharmas with no self, person, being, or life-span one attains anuttarā-bodhi; and it further says that what the Tathāgata calls good dharmas are not good dharmas, and so are called good dharmas — thus even the mark of good dharmas is not grasped. This is called ultimate cultivation. To cultivate thus is called ultimate because it accords with the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas. Hence it is judged to be about progressive cultivation.

You should know that it is called progressive cultivation rather than initial cultivation because the term carries deep meaning. It makes clear that this is a cultivation that advances deeply, and it also makes clear that all the meanings taught above were not merely about generating faith and opening understanding, not about beginning to practice. There is one more meaning that must not go unknown: faith, understanding, and practice cannot be definitively said to have no sequence, nor definitively said to have a sequence. A person must first have faith before inquiring into the Buddhadharma; and must understand the true meaning of the Buddhadharma before knowing true practice. Here there is plainly a sequence of before and after. Yet to speak truthfully: if one has no practice whatever, then one’s obstructions are deep and one’s wisdom shallow, and one can never grasp the very profound Buddhadharma. The more one’s practice advances, the deeper one’s understanding of principle becomes accordingly. And without understanding and practice, one’s faith too is as if present and as if absent; it cannot be called a fulfilled root of faith. From this, faith, understanding, and practice advance together at once — how can one speak of a sequence of before and after? One sometimes meets people who have faith in the Buddha for no apparent reason, or who never studied Buddhism before yet understand as soon as they hear the very profound Dharma; and there are those who understand not a whit of the Buddhadharma yet can arouse the mind and practice with vigor and courage. All these had practice in former lives, and meeting the present conditions it now comes forth; it is not accidental. Take realization itself: to realize is to verify. Whatever one has seen with one’s own eyes and done with one’s own person is called realization. Hence only when one has truly done it in accordance with the Dharma is it named practice; only when one has truly seen the Buddha’s principle is it named understanding; only when one truly knows the benefit of taking refuge in the Three Jewels is it named faith. Thus the single phrase “faith, understanding, practice” already contains the meaning of realization; only it is not usually named realization. It is for realizing the dharmakāya alone that the word “realization” is reserved. So we see this is a distinction in names only; in actuality, there is nowhere that is not realization. Even speaking of realizing the dharmakāya — what is such realization? It is nothing but the effect of the two matters of understanding and practice. When understanding and practice are carried to the ultimate, it is called ultimate realization. Apart from understanding and practice there is no realization to speak of. Nor is that all: this sutra says that when the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born. True reality is the dharmakāya. In other words, the manifestation of the dharmakāya is nothing but the purity of the mind of faith. From this, not only do faith, understanding, practice, and realization have no sequence of before and after; in the names and marks there seem to be four different matters, while in actuality there is no difference at all. The four matters are transformed into one, and this is called equality. From these four words alone one may awaken to the principle that equality reveals difference and difference reveals equality.

Taking one step further: when true reality manifests, there is only purity. Even the two words “mind of faith” leave no trace — then it is truly ultimate equality, unmoving and such. Therefore, if one understands the Buddha’s principle, then whatever single matter one picks up, one can exhaust it to its ultimate ground and return to equality. Take, for instance, the phrase in the passage on generating faith, “in a single thought one gives rise to pure faith”: spoken in terms of the marks of the matter of generating faith, it is called being in accord in a single thought, not yet pure mindfulness continuing without interruption. But if one speaks of its ultimate meaning, then this single phrase can be deep beyond any bottom and wide beyond any bound. Why so? Generating pure faith is the same as generating a pure mind, and has the same flavor of meaning as the purity of the mind of faith. “A single thought” means only this one thought. This thought is nothing other than the purity of faith; “generating” is manifesting. Then generating pure faith is the manifestation of a pure mind. Spoken thus, this single phrase is the realization of the unmoving, such-like essence of nature. Every other phrase and sentence may be grasped in the same way. This is why, hearing a single word or half a verse, one may realize the Way. This principle must not go unknown. Yet when expounding the sutra and teaching the Dharma, one sometimes cannot but speak in accordance with the surface marks of the text. If one stated this deep meaning at the very outset, hearers would instead have nothing to follow. This principle too must not go unknown. When this phrase was explained earlier, the reason the principle could not suddenly be made clear was this. Now that the teaching has reached an ever deeper level, there is no harm in picking it out along the way, so that people may know that in the Buddhadharma there is nothing shallow that is not also deep, and the deep can also be shallow — there is simply no shallow or deep, no sequence, to be spoken of. Hence one must not grasp its marks, and so it is said to be “neither is it” — not so. Yet in order to receive and guide living beings and to inspire them to advance, one cannot but provisionally posit a sequence of shallow and deep, along with all kinds of adorned and majestic matters. Hence one must not annihilate its marks, and so it is said to be “is named” — named so.

Hold on — today I am not explaining the sutra text but laying down the brush to go off the topic, rambling on about faith, understanding, practice, and realization at such length. To what purpose? You should know this is not idle talk. It is to bring out the meaning of the four words spoken above, “there is no fixed Dharma,” which runs through everything, so that the great assembly may grasp this meaning and find a way in everything they meet. I have taken faith, understanding, practice, and realization as the occasion, to show that this holds for all matters, not for the Buddhadharma alone. And from here on, the meaning enters ever deeper and subtler realms. If one does not gain even a little of this meaning, the mind cannot be lively, and the deep, subtle meanings will be hard to grasp. You should know that the fourfold passage below, “prajñā is not prajñā,” precisely makes plain that there is no fixed Dharma. My speaking thus is to prepare the way for what follows. You should know that because there is no fixed Dharma, one must not cling to existence nor cling to nothingness. Wherever the sutra says “is not,” it makes clear that existence must not be clung to. Not clinging to existence is to bring one back to the essence of nature. Why? Because nature is originally without marks, like empty space. How can it be sought through names and words? One must leave marks and turn the light inward, and then one may realize and enter. Wherever it says “is called,” it shows that nothingness must not be clung to. Not clinging to nothingness means that although one returns to nature, one does not destroy the names and marks of provisional existence. Why? Because nature is originally without marks yet is not without any mark. Marks are the function of the essence of nature; where there is essence there must be function. The essence of empty space is indeed utterly void, yet all phenomena in their teeming array — all marks of dependent and principal karmic fruits — appear from within it. Were there no phenomena, it would be a dead void, and it would not suffice to show that it is empty space. Yet if one does not grasp its marks, what harm does that do to empty space? How can one say it is absolutely without marks, and why should one need to annihilate its marks? Holding to this meaning in practice, one knows that to see the original nature one must leave names and cut off marks and break one’s view of self. If the view of self is not removed, one gives rise to discriminating mind, and as soon as a thought arises one grasps marks. And this view of self is a root of disease from beginningless time, hard to break. One must, in accordance with what the Buddha taught, on the one hand look back and shine within, stilling the climbing and deluded thoughts; and on the other hand follow the various rites and practices — bowing, repentance, giving, observing precepts, and so on — seeking to dissolve karmic obstructions and open one’s original wisdom. Thus faith grows, understanding and practice are accomplished, and one hopes that obstructions are cleared and nature appears. In practice one should also keep the mind from grasping at form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas. Realizing that the nature of this one thought of mind is one body with all Buddhas and living beings, and that its essence is originally void and still — then response is swift as a spirit, and accomplishment comes easily. When cultivating the cause one can neither grasp marks nor annihilate marks, clinging to neither of the two extremes of emptiness and existence, and so accord with the middle way; hence the response is great and the accomplishment is great. Therefore after accomplishment one can, without moving from the bodhimaṇḍa, make the body pervade the ten directions and manifest all kinds of adorned lands to save boundless and limitless living beings universally. This is what is meant by “without marks yet not without any mark, doing nothing yet doing everything.”

Extending this: hold to this meaning in one’s dealings with people, and one can be broad-minded and open-hearted, free of affliction and at ease. One also knows to speak carefully and act prudently, to go wrong in neither cause nor effect, and to be without hindrance. Hold to this meaning in dealing with the world, and one knows that all things are empty and have nothing to do with me — let the wind and waves rise as they will, I sit steady in my fishing boat. One also knows that human feelings and worldly ways tangle and turn endlessly, that safety and danger, sorrow and joy, come as they may, and one is at peace wherever one is. Hold to this meaning in bearing great responsibility and undertaking great matters: because one does not grasp marks, though matters come and one responds to them, the heavenly lord within is calm and unmoved. Because marks are not annihilated, though the mind grasps no marks, everything is orderly and nothing is neglected. Is this not “is not” and “is called,” a way in everything one meets? Truly it is as said: the Way is not far from man; it is man who puts it far from himself. Our Buddha came precisely to save the world, so whatever he taught encompasses all, worldly and world-transcending alike. One need only blend and comprehend this true meaning, and then every matter can be received and upheld, every moment is practice, everywhere there is benefit, and every place is the Buddhadharma. This is why the Buddhadharma is called the treasure of the Dharma, and why this sutra is above all the supreme treasure of the Dharma. So let me gather up my idle words and proclaim this supreme treasure of the Dharma.

(Ren) Next, the instruction. This has three parts: (Gui) first, a general instruction on the name and on upholding; next, a detailed explanation of the reason; third, a concluding revelation of the merit of upholding. (Gui, first) again has two parts: (Zi) first, revealing the name that can cut; next, revealing the method of upholding the sutra.
(Zi) First, revealing the name that can cut.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “This sutra is named the Vajra Prajñā Pāramitā.”

These seven characters are the overall title of the whole sutra; their meaning was explained in detail when the title was opened, so here I will speak of them briefly. Prajñā is rendered here as wisdom. With respect to cause it is called “understanding” (hui), with respect to fruit “wisdom” (zhi). Cause and fruit are one suchness, so the meaning is rendered together as wisdom. Pāramitā is rendered as “reaching the other shore.” With this wisdom one can end birth and death and enter nirvāṇa. Explained thus, pāramitā is nothing other than prajñā. Again, this wisdom is not the same as worldly cleverness and eloquence; it is Buddha-wisdom and Buddha-insight, the so-called knowledge and vision of the Buddha — the wisdom that reaches the other shore. Explained thus, prajñā is nothing other than pāramitā. “Vajra” is a metaphor. The vajra among things is the hardest and sharpest, able to cut through everything. Because it is hard, no thing can destroy it; because it is sharp, it can destroy every thing. It is used to illustrate how prajñā-pāramitā is like a great mass of fire, untouchable from any side, able to cut off all afflictions. What are afflictions? They are the delusions of view and of thought. Delusions of view are the views of self, of extremes, of error, and the two kinds of grasping; the most important are the view of self and the view of extremes. The view of self is the view of a self. In the Small Vehicle it refers specifically to the physical body falsely assembled from the four elements and five aggregates; in the Great Vehicle it extends to the self of dharmas. If one grasps the marks of dharmas or the marks of non-dharmas, one grasps self, person, being, and life-span; hence “self of dharmas.” Person, being, and life-span all arise from grasping a self, so to speak of self is to include the rest. The view of extremes: in the Small Vehicle it refers specifically to the views of annihilation and permanence that arise from the view of self; in the Great Vehicle it refers as well to the two extremes of the existence and emptiness of all dharmas. To cling to existence is to grasp dharmas, which is the view of permanence; to cling to emptiness is to grasp non-dharmas, which is the view of annihilation. Delusions of thought are greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt; these are the root, and from them arise stinginess, envy, and the rest. These root afflictions are all roots of disease from beginningless time, deeply ingrained habits, so that one revolves through the six paths and suffers without end. To escape this suffering one must cut off this root of disease. How is it cut off? Only by relying on this vajra sword of wisdom. Moreover, this portion was spoken at the ninth assembly of the Great Prajñā Sutra. All the assemblies teach prajñā, and all can cut. Here alone the name “vajra” is added to this portion, which shows that the meaning of this portion is especially essential and precise — harder, sharper, and more able to cut.
(Zi) Next, revealing the method of upholding the sutra.
“With this name you should receive and uphold it.”

These eight characters tell one to receive and uphold by understanding the meaning from the name and realizing the essence through the name; they do not mean to uphold the mere name. Lest people misunderstand, the Buddha then explains the reason himself. You should know that the meaning made plain in this sutra is in every case “one should dwell nowhere.” And the disease of living beings is that they grasp everywhere. Grasping is the meaning of dwelling. Because this disease of living beings is so deep, the Buddha opened by speaking of subduing the mind. Wherever he says “should not grasp,” “should not dwell,” it is the meaning of subduing. Now he says further: “With this name you should receive and uphold it.” This is no different from saying that you should receive and uphold the meaning that can cut, and put it into practice; and no different from saying that you should receive and uphold the vajra prajñā in order to subdue.

Among the delusions of view and thought, the view of self is the root. It is because of this that one grasps everywhere; because of this that one gives rise to all kinds of delusion, creates all kinds of karma, and suffers all kinds of pain; and because of this that one must urgently cut it off. When the view of self is removed, the obstruction of afflictions (that is, delusion) is removed, and the obstruction of karma and the obstruction of retribution are removed along with it. When the three obstructions are dissolved, the three bodies — dharma, reward, and response — appear in full. Hence to receive and uphold thus is to solve the matter at the root and gain the ultimate supreme fruit; how could it be merely to escape birth and death! This is why, wherever this sutra is, the place is honored, and in whomever it is, the person is honored. How fortunate we are to hear this supreme sutra Dharma; we must long since have planted good roots in the presence of immeasurable thousands of myriads of Buddhas. What cause for rejoicing — how can we recklessly belittle ourselves! Yet with good roots such as these, we still drag about this stinking bag of skin and sink and float in the sea of suffering. Surely through many lives we either slighted it and never read or recited it, or recited it without being able to receive and uphold it, or received and upheld it without being able to do so in accordance with the Dharma. Thinking of this, what shame is ours! Now by good fortune the Buddha’s light shines upon us, and again we hear this Dharma and read this sutra. If we are still as slack and careless as before, the road ahead is vast and vague, and who knows how many more times we must revolve, bringing ourselves suffering. Thinking of this, what dread comes over us! The ancients said: if this body is not saved in this life, in what other life will it be saved? Fearful, fearful!

Here the two characters “cut” and “uphold” carry a particularly important meaning. “Cut” means to decide and sever; “uphold” means to hold firmly. As said above, one should not dwell in the six dusts while giving rise to the mind. But ordinary people cannot match their strength to their wish: they know they should not dwell, yet unknowingly and unwittingly the mind sticks to things. Once the mind sticks, it is bound by them and cannot shake free. One must therefore keep “not dwelling in the six dusts while giving rise to the mind” in the heart, and at all times contemplate and observe the arising of thoughts and intentions. If one comes even slightly into contact with the six dusts, one should decide and sever on the spot. To sever on the spot means not to fear difficulty, not to seek easy comfort: it is the meaning of courage. One must further persist without slackening. Persistence is the meaning of diligence. Diligence means advancing with precise scrutiny, shining inward closely and intently, not letting the slightest thing go. It means advancing finely and meticulously, stilling the mind and calming thought, examining what is hidden and subtle. It means advancing with utter sincerity, praying most earnestly that the Three Jewels take pity and receive one, emit light and bless one, and lend one their strength. That recitation of the Buddha’s name brings no power is entirely because one has not applied effort here. In our practice we must, toward all defiling conditions — the so-called six dusts — follow this sutra’s two meanings of “able to cut” and “receive and uphold,” and decide and sever on the spot, persisting without slackening. If we do not thus straighten our spines and plant our feet firmly, how can we subdue the habits of many lives spent turning from enlightenment and uniting with dust? If I do not subdue them, they will subdue me. Once this mind is defiled by dust, it is impure, and a single recitation of the Buddha will of course go poorly. If one can truly decide and sever on the spot and persist without slackening, then single-mindedness is possible, and rebirth in the Pure Land and direct entry into non-retrogression are not difficult. Strive, strive!

In sum: all that was said above about subduing the mind and about not dwelling in the six dusts and giving rise to a pure mind — all those various gateways of contemplation and practice — must be received and upheld with an understanding of the meaning of “able to cut” taught here, and only then will they be more powerful. It follows that the meaning made plain here is extremely important. Hence the later comparison of the sutra’s merit will also be entirely unlike the earlier ones.
(Gui) Next, a detailed explanation of the reason. This has two parts: (Zi) first, a general heading; next, a detailed explanation.
(Zi) First, the general heading.
“Why is this so?”

The four characters “why is this so?” are a heading. What follows will explain in full the reason for receiving and upholding what can cut; hence they are raised first to draw attention. Commentators have always assigned this sentence to the passage in which the Buddha speaks of prajñā; I hold that it governs the two sections that follow. For both sections below teach the method of cultivation, and so both explain the reason why one should receive and uphold with this name. How can it be assigned to one passage only, leaving the rest of the text like scattered sand? Then the meaning that the comparison shows the sutra’s merit to be more supreme than before would have no footing either, which is quite unacceptable. Hence I here make these four characters a separate section, judged as “general heading,” to make clear that they govern the two sections below and are not confined to one passage within them. Surveying the meaning of the two sections below, one sees that this single sentence contains three meanings: (1) how is it cut? (2) from where does the cutting begin? (3) why must it be cut? I will speak of them in order.

What is meant by “how is it cut”? To cut is to cut off the view of self. The view of self appears everywhere; if one does not seize its essential point, how can one cut it? Moreover, the view of self is another name for deluded thought. And deluded thought is originally a transformation of the true mind; it cannot be cut off in itself. What is called cutting is only breaking it. How then can it be broken? By understanding principle, by opening understanding. Consider the seven characters of the sutra’s name, Vajra Prajñā Pāramitā. Vajra is hard and sharp, the so-called ability to cut; yet it is used to illustrate the five characters below, prajñā-pāramitā. Prajñā is wisdom; pāramitā is reaching the other shore. The wisdom that reaches the other shore is to say, wisdom that is thoroughgoing. From this it is clear that cutting off the view of self has no other method: it lies solely in understanding principle thoroughly — that is, in opening understanding thoroughly.

What principle, then, does “understanding principle thoroughly” mean understanding? You should know that living beings grasp everywhere for no other reason than that they do not know that the four elements and five aggregates, and all dharmas, are all produced by conditions, like illusions and transformations. Taking their own preconceived views as fixed and immovable, they cling and will not let go. This is called the view of self. Hence to break this view one should first understand that all dharmas are originally without fixity. Contemplating thus for a long time, one knows: since dharmas have no fixity, how can they be grasped? And since they have no fixity, what benefit is there in grasping them? If one can be without grasping toward all dharmas, the view of self dissolves of itself. This is the true vajra that breaks deluded views. “Understanding principle” means understanding this principle; understanding it, one can break the view of self, and that is what “thoroughly” means. Hence: “With this name you should receive and uphold it.” To comply with and uphold the vajra prajñā-pāramitā as one’s practice means to comply with this name and meaning and make it one’s contemplation. You should know that this portion of the sutra Dharma is precisely prajñā-pāramitā, yet the Buddha says it is not prajñā-pāramitā. The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma at every moment, yet says there is nothing taught; even atoms, worlds, and the thirty-two marks are all said to be not so, and merely called so. All of this is to reveal the meaning that there is no fixed Dharma. This is the first point.

What is meant by “from where does the cutting begin”? It should begin with the dharmas most intimate to oneself, contemplating them diligently so as to break one’s delusion. Prajñā-pāramitā is what practitioners should cultivate; yet one should know that it is not so, and leave the mark of names. The World-Honored One’s words are what practitioners should comply with; yet one should know that nothing is taught, and leave the mark of words. The great chiliocosm is the realm of the Buddha’s teaching; the thirty-two marks are the body manifested by the Buddha. Toward all of these one should be unattached; then all the rest may be known. This is what is called putting the brush to the page from a high place. Extending this: whatever dharmas one cultivates, whatever matters one undertakes, and one’s dependent and principal rewards — all should be contemplated by this meaning. This is the second point.

What is meant by “why must it be cut”? Consider the text below, where it says “the Buddha says” and “the Tathāgata says.” From this one knows that if one does not contemplate in this way and cut off one’s view of self, one contravenes the Buddha’s intent and cannot see the Tathāgata. This is the third point. With these three meanings clear, one knows the reason for receiving and upholding in this way.

(Zi) Next, the detailed explanation. This has two parts: (Chou) first, revealing the return to the essence of nature; next, revealing the non-destruction of provisional names. (Chou) first again has two parts: (Yin) first, revealing that one should uphold it while leaving the mark of names; next, revealing that one should uphold it while leaving the mark of words.
(Yin) First, revealing that one should uphold it while leaving the mark of names.
“Subhūti, when the Buddha speaks of prajñā-pāramitā, it is not prajñā-pāramitā.”

The current circulating editions contain the sentence “it is called prajñā-pāramitā.” This was added by later people and is a great error. You should know that this section and the next precisely make plain the return to the essence of nature, and so both dispense with marks in order to reveal nature. Only the two sections on the great chiliocosm and the thirty-two marks also make plain the non-destruction of provisional names. The section divisions are clear. Yet the ignorant made reckless additions, indiscriminately inserting phrases — how lamentable! Not only do the Tang dynasty manuscript sutras lack this sentence, the commentaries of the three great masters Zhiyi, Jiazang, and Guifeng contain no such sentence or meaning either. One should follow the ancient text.

To say “is not” is to cause one to leave marks. Leaving marks is the means of realizing nature. Hence the section is headed “return to the essence of nature.” Following the pattern of what came above, it should say “the Tathāgata says.” That it here says “the Buddha says” rather than “the Tathāgata says” carries a deeper meaning. Let me briefly state two points.

(1) “Buddha” is the name of the fruit of ultimate enlightenment. Everyone knows that one becomes a Buddha by realizing the fruit of ultimate enlightenment through cultivating prajñā; no one knows that it is in truth because cultivating prajñā is not prajñā. If one cultivates prajñā yet does not leave the mark of names, one is grasping self, person, being, and life-span — can one still be called ultimately enlightened? Is there any possibility of becoming a Buddha? Hence the Buddha deliberately says “the Buddha says,” to show that the one who realizes the fruit realizes it by this, and so the one cultivating the cause should cultivate in this way.

(2) Having realized nature, one also manifests marks, and so is called a Buddha. Thus the appellation “Buddha” is a name that fully reveals both nature and marks, unlike “Tathāgata,” which is only a name for the virtue of nature. Hence the present “the Buddha says” points out that prajñā and not-prajñā must not be split into two. “Not prajñā-pāramitā” must be carried out from within prajñā-pāramitā. So the instruction is: right at the name, leave the name. Hence the earlier words: “With this name you should receive and uphold it.” This has the same flavor as the sentence “one should give rise to a pure mind.” It is what is meant by “emptiness within existence,” not annihilating existence to reveal emptiness. Because the World-Honored One is precisely making nature plain, he cannot but dispense with marks; yet if he dispensed with them wholesale, he feared people would misunderstand and fall into one-sided emptiness. Hence he says “the Buddha says” rather than “the Tathāgata says,” to convey the meaning. This, and the fact that when he does not destroy provisional names and says “is called such and such” he says “the Tathāgata says” rather than “the Buddha says,” are both devices of the deepest subtlety. For when he does not destroy provisional names and says “the Tathāgata says,” he makes clear that although marks are not destroyed, one should still return to nature. And now when he dispenses with them and says “the Buddha says” rather than “the Tathāgata says,” he makes clear that although one should return to nature, marks are not thereby destroyed. Thus the meaning of not destroying provisional names is already contained here. Why need one recklessly add the sentence “is called prajñā-pāramitā” to show that provisional names are not destroyed? All this comes of not understanding the sutra’s meaning, and so of ignorant, reckless fabrication. In sum: the Buddha’s speaking of prajñā is spoken according to the principle and wisdom of his own realization, to enable all living beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. To open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is to enable them to know that nature is originally without marks, and that one must leave marks in one’s cultivation before one can see nature; hence “prajñā is not prajñā.” If one does not understand this principle and harbors in the mind the name and mark of prajñā-pāramitā, one is grasping the marks of dharmas — can one still be said to receive and uphold prajñā-pāramitā? Why not? Because if one grasps the marks of dharmas, one is grasping self, person, being, and life-span. Here it says only that prajñā-pāramitā is not prajñā-pāramitā, without joining the two characters “vajra” to the statement, precisely to make clear that the earlier words about receiving and upholding “with this name” mean that one should receive the name of vajra’s ability to cut in order to carry out the reality of vajra’s ability to cut, and so cut off one’s grasping of the marks of dharmas. If prajñā, the supreme Dharma, should still leave the mark of names, how much more so all other dharmas! You should also know that the Buddha says this precisely to cause one not to grasp the marks of dharmas, so that in cultivating all dharmas every dharma is prajñā, and only then is it prajñā-pāramitā. This is why it was said above that there is no fixed Dharma for the Tathāgata to teach. In sum: “when the Buddha speaks of prajñā, it is not prajñā” is to cause one to comprehend that every dharma is prajñā, and that one must not cling to the name and mark of prajñā. This is the reason for receiving and upholding “with this name” — not for upholding the name itself. Moreover, the words “the reason” are the true meaning; the earlier “you should receive and uphold it” means that one should receive the true meaning and put it into practice.
(Yin) Next, revealing that one should uphold it while leaving the mark of words.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata taught any Dharma?” Subhūti said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has taught nothing.”

This question follows on the text above. Someone might ask: one should not dwell in the mark of the dharma of prajñā-pāramitā, yet this dharma was originally taught by the Buddha. When he taught it, was there no mark of dharma? If there were no mark of dharma, how could he teach it? To guard against this doubt, the Buddha asked this question. “Has he taught any Dharma?” means: does the mind harbor the mark of the dharma of prajñā-pāramitā that has been taught? The World-Honored One’s question already contains the word “no.” Why? “Tathāgata” is a name for the virtue of nature. The essence of nature is void and still — how could it have a taught mark of dharma? That he says “the Tathāgata says” rather than “the Buddha says” is meant to make this clear. (Again, the Buddha’s manifestation of marks is precisely for the sake of teaching the Dharma; had he said “the Buddha says,” it would conflict with the meaning of “nothing taught.” Hence this section can only say “the Tathāgata says,” not “the Buddha says.”)

Wherever the phrase “Subhūti said to the Buddha” is marked, it shows that the words are most important and must not be neglected. The answer goes a step further, saying that not only is there no taught dharma, there is nothing taught at all. “Nothing taught” means there is nothing that is taught, not that there is no teaching. (Sentences such as “nothing practiced,” “nothing attained” have the same meaning.) For the essence of nature is self-verified, and that is named Tathāgata. “Tathāgata” makes clear that he has realized the essence of equal nature. Equal means that principle and wisdom are one suchness, and subject and object are one suchness. (Hence the later text speaks of “the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas.”) Since he has realized this one suchness, his words are named “such-speaking.” (Hence the later text says “the Tathāgata is one who speaks what is such.”) “Such-speaking” makes clear that the words flow freely out of the ocean of the nature of equal suchness. He never gave rise to a thought or an intention; though he speaks all day, speaks blazingly, speaks in every mote, speaks in every dust, in truth there is no mark of speaking. Since there is not even a mark of speaking, how could there be a taught mark of dharma? Hence “the Tathāgata has taught nothing.” This exchange of question and answer not only blocks doubt; it is also meant to cause those who receive and uphold to realize that the essence of nature has not only no mark of names but also no mark of words. Let them also know that the Tathāgata speaks blazingly yet has no mark of speaking. Then they will know that one who receives and upholds the taught Dharma should cultivate blazingly yet without the marks of dharmas.

Taking these two sections together: to realize the essence of nature one must leave the marks of names and words. But how, after all, are names and words to be left? If one does not know this, one knows only that it is so, not why it is so. You should know that in these two sections the World-Honored One in truth causes those who receive and uphold to leave thought. If thought is not left, the marks of names and words can never be left. How do we know? A passage in the “Gate of the Mind in Suchness” in the Awakening of Faith can prove it. The treatise says: “If one is free from thought, there are no marks of any objective realm.” It also says: “Free from the mark of words, free from the mark of names, free from the mark of conceptual activity, ultimately equal, and finally nothing but one mind — therefore it is called suchness.” Here “suchness” is another name for the essence of nature. Of the three phrases — free from the mark of words, and so on — the weight falls on “free from the mark of conceptual activity.” This phrase means leaving thought. For “activity” is climbing; conceptual activity of the mind is the arising of thoughts and intentions. If a thought of mind moves, it must have something to climb upon, and so it falls into the mark of names. And words are the voice of the mind: the mind must first climb upon what it wishes to say, and only then does it reach words. So if a thought of mind moves, it also falls into the mark of words. Hence of the three phrases, “free from the mark of conceptual activity” is the general one. Once the mark of conceptual activity is left, the marks of names and of words are both left. This accords with the sentence earlier in the treatise: “If one is free from thought, there are no marks of any objective realm.”

Free from thought, and there are no marks of any objective realm. Hence, free from the mark of conceptual activity, one is ultimately equal, nothing but one mind, and this is called suchness. By this meaning of the treatise we verify the meaning of the sutra: then “causing one to uphold while leaving the marks of names and words” here is precisely causing one to cultivate while leaving thought. The treatise also cites another sutra: “One who can contemplate no-thought is tending toward Buddha-wisdom.” Buddha-wisdom is prajñā-pāramitā. Hence this Vajra Prajñā Pāramitā Sutra should be received and upheld by thus cutting off the climbing deluded thoughts that cling to names and words. This is the reason for “with this name you should receive and uphold it.”

The Awakening of Faith also says: “You should know that defiled dharmas and pure dharmas are all mutually dependent; no self-mark can be spoken of. Therefore all dharmas, from the very beginning, are neither form nor mind, neither wisdom nor consciousness, neither existent nor nonexistent; ultimately no mark can be spoken of. And as for there being words, you should know that this is the Tathāgata’s skillful means, provisionally using words to guide living beings. Its purport is always to leave thought and return to suchness, because thinking of all dharmas causes the mind to arise and perish and prevents entry into true wisdom.” This passage from the treatise is even better cited as a gloss for these two sections of sutra text.

This great section on requesting instruction about the name and about upholding is of crucial importance. Now I should rely once more on this passage from the treatise and explain it in detail, so that it may be thoroughly understood. Only when the principle is clearly seen can one contemplate and apply effort; I think this is what you all wish to hear.

First, the three phrases: neither form nor mind, neither wisdom nor consciousness, neither existent nor nonexistent. In “neither form,” the word “form” covers manifest form, unmanifest form, and so on. Manifest form means dharmas having shape that can be pointed to; unmanifest form means dharmas without shape that can be pointed to. These various dharmas, whether manifest or unmanifest, originally have no self-essence; their essence is only mind — hence “neither form.” Yet they are merely what mind manifests; they are not in fact mind — hence “neither mind.” The “wisdom” in “neither wisdom” means the wisdom of nature. The essence of nature is equal and void and still; how could it have any dharmas? Hence “neither wisdom.” Are dharmas, then, consciousness? You should know they are merely what consciousness manifests; one cannot say dharmas are consciousness. Hence “neither consciousness.” “Neither existent nor nonexistent”: when causes and conditions gather, dharmas seem to arise, so they are not nonexistent; yet being produced by conditions they are illusory marks, so they are not existent. These three phrases together say that all dharmas are merely set against one another in mutual contrast, seeming to exist while in truth not existing, empty right where they are. This explains the meaning of the words above: “you should know that defiled dharmas and pure dharmas are all mutually dependent; no self-mark can be spoken of.”

You should know that prajñā too is only so named in contrast to those dharmas. Because all dharmas are produced by conditions and illusorily exist, originally without self-mark, how could any self-mark be spoken of? How can one cling to the mark of names? Hence “prajñā is not prajñā.” And because the Buddha has realized the true wisdom of suchness, though he speaks blazingly there is in truth no mark of words; hence “the Tathāgata has taught nothing.” Only for the sake of living beings does he provisionally use words to guide them, causing them to leave thought and realize nature. From this one knows that the sutra’s saying “prajñā is not prajñā,” causing one to leave the mark of names, and again “nothing is taught,” causing one to leave the mark of words — is their purport not to cause the assembly to leave thought and return to suchness? Then what is meant by receiving and upholding is that one should receive and uphold the vajra that cuts off deluded thought, as is now clear.

It was said above that clearly understanding that there is no fixed Dharma clears the source of the view of self; now it is said that breaking climbing deluded thought cuts off the stream of the view of self. Consider the last few sentences of the passage cited above from the treatise: “because thinking of all dharmas causes the mind to arise and perish and prevents entry into true wisdom.” True wisdom is the essence of nature. From this one sees that nature is originally without thought; to realize the essence of nature one must cut off thought. One also sees that the arising of a thought is the mind of birth and death, and that because there is a mind of birth and death the fruit of birth and death is summoned. If one does not cut off thought, how can one end birth and death? Yet all living beings, from beginningless time, have had thought follow thought in unbroken succession, never once free of thought. This is called beginningless ignorance. Ignorance is non-awakening. Because of non-awakening, thought arises. What is non-awakening? It is what is called not penetrating the one dharma-realm: not comprehending that the principle and phenomena of the ten dharma-realms are solely one suchness, one substance, equal. This is non-awakening. Since one does not awaken to equal, one-substance reality, one’s thoughts move. When thought moves, the seer and the seen arise accordingly, and so there are marks of self and other, of difference. From this, discrimination never ceases, grasping and calculating continue, all kinds of karma are created, all kinds of suffering are summoned. And again, pervading and permeating each other, fruit turns back into cause, and cause receives further fruit. Ever more deeply deluded, one sinks and does not return. Now, wishing to return to the root and go back to the source, one must solve the matter at the root and cut off thought. Hard, hard! Because it is hard, the World-Honored One taught all kinds of skillful means so that beings might accord with them and enter. As cited above, “one who can contemplate no-thought is entering Buddha-wisdom” — this too is one of the skillful means. This is the critical juncture of birth and death for us all, the most important and urgent matter; it is also what this sutra causes us to receive and uphold. I do not shrink from prolixity, and will speak further of the skillful means.

You should know that the three words “contemplate no-thought” are indeed a skillful means. But how is one to contemplate? One still needs a skillful means in order to give rise to contemplation. What is the skillful means for cultivating contemplation? The Awakening of Faith has spoken of it. The treatise says: “You should know that because all dharmas cannot be spoken and cannot be thought, they are called suchness. Question: if such is the meaning, how can living beings accord with it and be able to enter? Answer: if one knows that all dharmas, though spoken of, have nothing that can speak and nothing that can be spoken; though thought of, have nothing that can think and nothing that can be thought — this is called according with it. If one is free from thought, it is called entering.” “Because all dharmas cannot be spoken and cannot be thought, they are called suchness” — this makes suchness plain in terms of all dharmas. The meaning is that all dharmas have no substance; their substance is only pure nature. (Pure nature is another name for suchness.) Since all dharmas have as their substance only pure nature — what is called “all dharmas are one suchness” — it is called the one true dharma-realm. For though the mind has no dharmas, dharmas arise from the mind; hence the dharmas of the ten dharma-realms are never apart from the one true mind. “One suchness,” “one true” — this is why the original nature is called suchness. Making suchness plain in terms of all dharmas makes the meaning of one-suchness and one-true very easy to understand. Such is the skillfulness of this way of speaking. Because all dharmas are one suchness, they cannot be spoken; because the true mind is without thought, they cannot be thought. Hence “all dharmas cannot be spoken and cannot be thought, and are called suchness.” The “such meaning” in the question refers to “cannot be spoken, cannot be thought.” Because living beings all have speaking and thinking, the question is how they can accord with it and enter. “According” is the meaning of skillful means. The question means: since living beings speak and think, and one wishes them to be without speech and without thought — without a skillful means, how can they realize and enter? In the answer, speaking and thinking are raised together; yet one who can be without thought will of course be without speech. Let us make it clear through the meaning of thought, and the meaning of speech will be clear of itself.

You should know that the sentence “though thought of, there is nothing that can think and nothing that can be thought” precisely points out the skillful means for cultivating contemplation. Hence it continues at once: “this is called according with it.” Why is this sentence the skillful means for contemplating no-thought? You should know it contains two meanings.

First, in terms of the essence of nature. You should know that thought is the karmic consciousness, and in the essence of nature there is no such thing at all. This is what is meant by “from the very beginning, free from the marks of all dharma-differences, because there is no deluded thought.” This makes clear that though the karmic consciousness stirs in confusion, the purity of nature remains as it is — just as when all phenomena teem in empty space, space itself remains as it is. This is an essential point and must not go unknown. Knowing it, one knows that nature and thought are originally apart, and one will not mistake a thief for one’s son.

Next, in terms of thought itself. You should know that thought as a thing arises right here and perishes right here, never pausing for an instant. The trouble is that as the former thought perishes, the latter thought arises again, thought following thought in succession. Only one without the skill of stillness does not notice the succession and mistakes the before and after for a single thought. If the before and after were truly a single thought, the practitioner would have no way to proceed. It is precisely because arising and perishing never cease that it is said: do not fear the arising of thought, only fear the lateness of awareness. This makes clear that thought arises and perishes as it goes, with no substantial thing — like a flower in the sky, illusorily existent and truly nonexistent. This too is an essential point that must not go unknown. Knowing it, one knows that thought itself is empty right where it is, and one will not grasp the void as real.

With these two meanings clear, one may at any time and in any place, in accordance with these two meanings, contemplate closely and intently. When a thought arises, rouse one’s spirit and reproach oneself: “Nature is originally without thought — where has this just come from?” With such a shining, the thought subsides of itself. A beginner without power of concentration will find a second thought suddenly arising within an instant; then reproach and illuminate again in the same way. In time, thoughts will visibly diminish day by day; even when they arise, their force will gradually weaken.

Question: to rouse awareness and illumination — is this not again giving rise to a thought? Answer: it is giving rise to a thought. You should know that since thought first stirred at beginningless time, the accumulated habit is deep and firm; to force it back and break it is very, very hard. One can only follow its habit without applying force, and instead switch to another thought to interrupt the original thought and prevent the succession. It is precisely because arising and perishing never cease that one can get a hold on it. You should further know that although contemplation and illumination are also thoughts, they are thoughts that arise as function in accord with the essence; one can therefore follow this function into the essence. They are utterly different in flavor from the thoughts that arise from losing the original nature. For the arising of thought is the same, but the function of the arising thought is vastly different. Because one knows that nature is originally without thought and that thought too is originally empty, one gives rise to the function of contemplation in order to remove deluded thought. This function arises in accord with the essence of nature, and so is utterly different from what arises from losing nature. This is called according with it; this is called skillful means. Yet you should know that this thought of contemplation is also illusory, also produced by conditions and without nature; it is now used merely to remove other thoughts. If one grasps this thought as real, it becomes a disease again. Prajñā-pāramitā is precisely the remedy for the disease of grasping; hence prajñā too must not be grasped. “Prajñā is not prajñā” makes clear that it should not be grasped. Prajñā originally contains three meanings: the prajñā of words, the prajñā of contemplation, and the prajñā of true reality. Through words one gives rise to contemplation and realizes true reality. And none of these three prajñās should be clung to. As for words: if one merely clings to the words without cultivating contemplation and practice, one is entirely within the mark of names. As for contemplation: if the mind harbors the thought of a contemplating subject and a contemplated object, one has not yet left the mark of names. And even when one realizes the prajñā of true reality, in truth there is nothing realized and nothing attained. If there is realization and attainment, one has still not left the mark of names, and it is not true reality; nor is it called prajñā-pāramitā. Hence “prajñā is not prajñā” here runs from beginning to end.

Returning to the source has no second road, but the skillful means are many gates. The one practice of reciting the Buddha’s name is especially the skillful means within skillful means for cutting off thought. Causing other thoughts to cease by reciting the Buddha’s name is likewise switching to another thought. And recitation is more intimate than cultivating contemplation: contemplation may be called wisdom-thought, while recitation is pure thought. One exchanges a pure, clean thought to cure the defiled, turbid thoughts one has always had, and further causes one to think single-mindedly — again using a single, undivided thought to cure the scattered, disordered thoughts one has always had. Moreover, “Buddha” means awakened: when every thought is the Buddha, every thought is awakening, and to be awakened is to awaken to the fact that nature is originally without thought — hence it is more intimate. Therefore one need only be diligent and single-minded to reach reciting without reciting. You should know that the aim of recitation must be to arrive at reciting without reciting. To arrive at no-thought is to arrive at suchness; then without speaking of cutting, it is cut, and without seeking realization, it is realized. How great a skillful means this is! Hence it is called the skillful means within skillful means.

What I just said — “without seeking realization, it is realized” — refers at first to realizing only one portion, because at that time only coarse thoughts are absent; subtle thoughts are still many. The Awakening of Faith says: “If one is free from thought, it is called entering.” “Entering” is realizing and entering. And this phrase is deep beyond the bottom. You should know that from contemplation and practice one reaches resemblance, and only then arrives at partial realization. Partial realization means realizing portion by portion; at first one enters only one portion. From there one passes through forty-one stages and reaches wondrous enlightenment, becoming a Buddha; only then are thoughts completely exhausted. Only when they are exhausted does one completely realize and enter the nature of suchness. Yet in truth there is no way to name this; it is provisionally called “entering.” Why? Because though attained, in truth nothing is attained; though entered, in truth nothing is entered. Only thus is it truly leaving thought, truly entering. As for the work of reciting the Buddha’s name: even if one cannot yet reach reciting without reciting, if one’s practice and vows are true and earnest, then by the power of Amitābha’s compassionate vows one is also received and reborn, and is then the same as avaivartika, which means non-retrogression. That is the stage of the first dwelling. To reach this stage by other practices would require long kalpas; here one life suffices to accomplish it. That it is the skillful means within skillful means needs no saying! You should know that “the same as avaivartika” makes clear that one’s own standing has not yet reached it, and that one attains non-retrogression only by being received by the Buddha’s power. How fortunate we are to hear this method — how can we waste time and let it slip through our fingers! Yet “true and earnest practice and vows” requires that the mind be single-mindedly fixed on reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth; only then is it true and earnest. If one recites the Buddha’s name with one hand while giving rise to dusty, turbid thoughts with the other, one’s practice and vows are not true and earnest. Hence one who recites the Buddha’s name, even if cutting off thought is not easy to accomplish, must certainly accomplish the two sentences: one should not dwell in form while giving rise to the mind, and one should not dwell in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas while giving rise to the mind. Otherwise one’s vows are not earnest and one’s practice is not true — how can one be received by the Buddha? Why? Because one’s dusty, turbid energy is heavy and utterly out of accord with the two words “pure and clean.” Then even the Buddha can do nothing.

In sum: deluded thoughts flying in confusion are the root of disease that living beings have had since beginningless time, and must never be forcibly suppressed. If forcibly suppressed, one’s vital energy is injured instead. For deluded thought is nothing other than the function of the original mind; it is only that it has been misused, and so has become a disease. One need only follow the Buddhadharma and switch it over, returning it to wisdom-thought or pure thought; in time it returns of itself to no-thought. Then it is the wisdom of equality and the wisdom of wondrous observation. When the sutra says “cut off,” you should know it means removing the disease, not removing the dharma. The word “cut” means cutting off the deluded so that it returns to the true. If one can return to the true, one suddenly awakens greatly, comprehending that all dharmas are one suchness and are originally the one true dharma-realm, originally without differences of self and other. Then ten thousand thoughts melt away. This is why one can only use the method of switching thoughts. From this one knows that calling the switching of thoughts a “skillful means” is still a provisional, expedient expression; in truth it is the fundamental method of rescue. Apart from it there is no other method. This principle must not go unknown.

Even speaking of cutting off the deluded and returning to the true, one must advance gradually. A beginner cannot be spoken to of this all at once. For living beings have been deluded about the true and chasing the deluded since beginningless time, drifting on and forgetting to return. It is like a prodigal son in the world who has long since wandered off and forgotten to come home: to draw him back one must guide him well and entice him, and only then is there hope. Otherwise one only adds trouble to the household. So it is here. One must read and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures much, to wake one from delusion and confusion; and must draw near to spiritual friends much, to open what is covered over and point out the road of practice. And in applying effort one must proceed from the shallow to the deep, and only then enter ever better states. Otherwise the mind is only further unsettled. This too must not go unknown.

Take this sutra itself: a thousand words and ten thousand phrases have been spoken above, and only here, as the first half nears its end, does it plainly cause one to leave thought. That one cannot overstep the stages and speak of this all at once is now quite clear. Yet you should also know that from the detailed talk onward, all the various gateways of contemplation and practice that were taught are in fact means of entering from the shallow to the deep, skillful means for leaving thought. For one’s practice must be cultivated to the point of no-thought before one can realize nature and attain the ultimate. Now, by this meaning, I will summarize what came before once more and point it out layer by layer, so that it may be blended and comprehended and one’s complete understanding opened.
What is called opening understanding is opening wisdom. Relying on the various sutras and treatises, the opening of understanding has three steps.

The first step is to cause the wisdom that knows objects to be empty to open. Because living beings do not know that all dust-objects are originally illusory and unreal, they grasp everywhere and the view of self springs up at random. So first one causes them to comprehend that the six dusts and other objects are only empty and without reality. If they know this, they can begin not to be deluded by them. Not being deluded is wisdom. Hence it is named the wisdom that knows objects to be empty.

The second step is to cause the wisdom of no-dust to open. “Dust” means the six dusts and other objects; “no” means that everything is only mind, and outside the mind there are no dharmas. One must penetrate this, and also gain the skillful means for sweeping away dust-objects; then gradually the heart comes to have not a speck of dust. If one can be without dust, the light of wisdom grows brighter. This is the wisdom of no-dust. When this wisdom is clear, even if thoughts arise they are extremely faint. Only then can one cut them. Cutting off thought also requires the wisdom of skillful means; it is named vajra wisdom. This is the third step.

Vajra means the ability to cut.
