Consider how, from the very opening, the Buddha caused one to arouse the vast mind and save all living beings, as if forgetting oneself: this is the very first skillful means. For all living beings, because they do not penetrate the one dharma-realm, unawares give rise to thought and so have ignorance; hence they draw the boundary between self and other most sharply and grasp it most tightly. Now the Buddha causes them to give up self and save others, to arouse the vast mind: this causes them to penetrate that the one true dharma-realm is originally without distinction of self and other, and so to dissolve the rigid, ingrained habit of discrimination. This works from the root of the very non-awakening from which thought originally arose. Hence it is called the very first skillful means. After he had spoken of not dwelling in form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas in giving, he explained it in terms of bodily marks: “all marks are delusive.” This causes one to observe that roots, body, environment, and realm are all dust-objects, all delusive marks, so as to open the wisdom that knows objects to be empty. You should know that the reason living beings discriminate self and other so unbreakably is simply that they are bound by objects and cannot let go; and the reason they cannot let go is simply that they mistake all kinds of objective marks for real. Now the Buddha wakes them: “all are delusive.” Truly this is cold water poured down the back, making one’s hair stand on end. This is the second skillful means.

What follows continues with observing the precepts and cultivating merit being able to generate faith, and taking this as real. This causes one to believe this true meaning and begin to practice; for observing the precepts and cultivating merit is the very first skillful means for beginning practice. If one can truly give rise to pure faith in a single thought, then one has already been able to understand and practice each of the things taught above. Why? Because without understanding and practice one cannot be in accord in a single thought. At this point one gains immeasurable merit. Why? Because being able to be in accord in a single thought means one has already gained the wisdom that knows objects to be empty, and the mind that dwells in marks and the view of self and other are thereby reduced. Then, going a step further, the Buddha tells one that if the mind grasps marks it is grasping self, person, being, and life-span, and that neither dharmas nor non-dharmas should be grasped. Grasping is giving rise to thought; to say that the mind should not grasp dharmas or non-dharmas already contains the meaning that one must not give rise to thoughts and intentions. He further tells one that dharmas are originally without fixity, and so cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken of, and that all worthies and sages are distinguished by the unconditioned Dharma. The unconditioned is the mind without arising and perishing; the mind of arising and perishing is thought. This is again to coax and entice one, saying: since you can truly believe, aspire to worthiness and sagehood, and be in accord in a single thought, you should further still the mind of arising and perishing. Below he speaks further of the greatness of the merit, to delight and move one. And when he has fully made it plain in terms of the fruit, he plainly points out the word “thought.” If one cannot form a thought when attaining the fruit, then one should not move a thought when cultivating the cause — this is clear. He concludes with “one should give rise to a pure mind.” What is giving rise to a pure mind? It is giving rise to the mind while dwelling nowhere amid dust-objects. This is a further step beyond what came before: from the wisdom that knows objects to be empty, the wisdom of no-dust is opened. Before, one only knew it; now one is caused to be without it — is that not a further advance? Yet opening the wisdom of no-dust is in truth the preparatory skillful means for finally opening vajra wisdom. As for practice, to cultivate from the wisdom that knows objects to be empty up to the wisdom of no-dust requires several kalpas. The former is the stage of contemplation and practice; the latter is the stage of resemblance. This wisdom is the pivot for turning from ordinary to sage. Without gaining the wisdom of no-dust, one cannot advance further to open vajra wisdom, and so cannot ascend to the stage of the first dwelling. Without ascending to the first dwelling, one cannot pass from the stage of resemblance into the stage of partial realization and become a sage. Hence the merit of gaining the wisdom of no-dust surpasses the former by immeasurable, boundless times. Why is the merit so great? Because you should know that such a person accomplishes the supreme, foremost, rarest Dharma. “Accomplishes” means accomplishes the wisdom of no-dust. If the mind can truly be without dust-objects, then even if thoughts arise they are fewer than before and their force is thinner. Only when practice has come this far can one attain to cutting off thought. Hence this section on requesting instruction about the name and about upholding next tells of the method for cutting off thought. The stages, shallow and deep, are strictly ordered. Such is the Buddha’s teaching. You should know that from the opening sentence, “one should thus subdue one’s mind,” down to the teaching that one should not dwell in form and so on while giving rise to the mind, all of it is subduing delusion. One must be able to subdue before one can cut. Here it plainly says, “receive and uphold with this name,” and the name is Vajra Prajñā. Hence all the meanings made plain here are opening one’s vajra wisdom.

Vajra means the ability to cut; leaving names and words means leaving thought. If vajra wisdom is not opened, how can thought be cut? You should know that one who ascends to the stage of the first dwelling must possess this wisdom. Without it, one cannot cut off ignorance. Ignorance is non-awakening; because of non-awakening, thought arises. Hence cutting off ignorance is cutting off thought. One must cut off one portion of ignorance to realize one portion of the dharmakāya and ascend to the first dwelling. From the first dwelling upward there is nothing but this wisdom growing step by step, so that ignorance is cut portion by portion, the dharmakāya realized portion by portion, and the stages rise portion by portion. Passing through forty stages, one reaches the final mind of the tenth ground; there this wisdom is harder and sharper still, and is named the vajra path, and one ascends to Equal Enlightenment (the forty-first stage). After ascending to Equal Enlightenment, one again uses this wisdom to cut off the last, most subtle portion of ignorance, and so ascends to Wondrous Enlightenment and becomes a Buddha. Usually the wisdom of Equal Enlightenment alone is taken as vajra wisdom; below Equal Enlightenment it is still called the wisdom of no-dust. In truth the name of this wisdom simply reveals its ability to cut. If one does not possess it, one cannot cut off one portion of ignorance, realize one portion of the dharmakāya, and ascend to the first dwelling. Hence all from the first dwelling upward in fact possess this wisdom; it is only that it increases in superiority stage by stage, until at Equal Enlightenment it is complete. Thus the wisdom of Equal Enlightenment alone bears this name. This principle must not go unknown. From what has been said above, one must reach a corresponding degree before one can cut off thought; and if thought is not cut off, one cannot realize the dharmakāya and turn from ordinary to sage. And before cutting off thought one must first cultivate all kinds of preparatory skillful means — this meaning is clear indeed.

From the detailed talk up to this point, this sutra has already summarized its meaning several times, and each summary makes plain one meaning. The reason for this is simply the wish that hearers blend and comprehend it and gain more benefit, and also to make clear that the meanings stored in the sutra are inexhaustible and can never be fully expounded. All the teaching given above is but a drop in the great ocean.

To summarize what has been made plain above concerning these two sections — leaving names and leaving words — so that it may be remembered: (1) One must first thoroughly understand that there is no fixed Dharma, to clear the source of deluded thought. This is wisdom. (2) One must further break the mind of climbing thought, to cut off the stream of deluded thought. This is the ability to cut. This is the reason for receiving and upholding with the name Vajra Prajñā Pāramitā. As for cultivating contemplation and reciting the Buddha’s name, these are skillful means for the ability to cut. These skillful means are still contained within the meaning of the two sections; they do not come from outside. “One who can contemplate no-thought is tending toward Buddha-wisdom.” Buddha-wisdom is that prajñā-pāramitā is not prajñā-pāramitā. The Buddha’s speaking of prajñā is to cause one to give rise to contemplation through words; receiving and upholding is to cause the assembly to do the work of contemplation; and leaving names and words is to cause them to leave thought. Is that not plainly causing them to contemplate no-thought? “Receive and uphold” carries the sense of holding it earnestly to the breast: that is, one should never forget the Buddha’s words and never contravene the Tathāgata, thought after thought. Never forgetting the Buddha’s words, thought after thought, is precisely single-minded recitation of the Buddha. Never contravening the Tathāgata, thought after thought, means not only reciting the response-body Buddha but also causing one to recite the dharmakāya, true-reality Buddha. Again, because of non-awakening, thought arises; causing one to understand thoroughly that there is no fixed Dharma is causing one to awaken. Hence it is called clearing the source, because non-awakening is the source from which thought arises. Next, causing one to break deluded thought is leaving thought; hence it is called cutting the stream, because the arising of thought comes forth from non-awakening. And after non-awakening and the arising of thought, there comes the division of seer and seen, forming marks of difference between self and other. Now the whole effort lies in remedying non-awakening and the arising of thought; that is, it works at the root of the view of self. Once the root is pulled out, the view of self is gone of itself. This is the reason why receiving and upholding cuts off the view of self.

Again, these two sections make plain the empty tathāgatagarbha. “Empty” has two meanings: (1) the essence of nature is originally empty; (2) one empties one’s deluded thoughts. Here “prajñā is not prajñā” and “the Tathāgata has taught nothing” speak of the essence of nature being originally empty; while leaving the mark of names and leaving the mark of words is emptying one’s deluded thoughts. Hence these two sections precisely make plain the meaning of the empty tathāgatagarbha. The two sections below make plain the non-empty tathāgatagarbha. “Empty” reveals essence; “non-empty” reveals function. The two sections below on not destroying provisional names are the means of revealing function, for roots, body, and world are all functions manifested by the virtue of nature; hence the meaning of the non-empty tathāgatagarbha.

(Chou) Next, revealing the non-destruction of provisional names. This has two parts: (Yin) first, revealing that one should uphold it while not grasping objects; next, revealing that one should uphold it while not grasping bodily marks. (Yin) first again has two parts: (Mao) first, question and answer; next, the direct revelation.
(Mao) First, question and answer.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms in a great trichiliocosm many?” Subhūti said: “Very many, World-Honored One.”

“Name” means a name. All dharmas have marks of difference; according to those differences names are established. Hence talk of names is talk in terms of marks. Marks are illusory existence, and so names are provisional names. “Illusory existence” makes clear that they are nonexistent yet exist, exist yet are nonexistent. “Not destroyed” means not annihilated. Marks are the function arising from essence — how can they be annihilated? Though not annihilated, marks are in truth not the essence, and so still should not be grasped. For essence does not change, while marks constantly change; essence is the root, marks are the branches. One should not abandon the root to chase the branches, or be deluded by marks and forget essence; hence one should not be attached. “Leaving” and “not attached” at first hearing seem the same, but on examination they differ. To have nothing to do with each other is called leaving; to manifest and function without being bound by it is called not attaching. The two sections above that say “leaving” make clear that the practitioner’s weight lies in realizing essence, and that essence and marks originally have nothing to do with each other. The two sections below that say “not attaching” further make clear that the practitioner should first realize essence, and clearly must also penetrate function and must not destroy marks. Yet although one penetrates function, one should in the end return to essence, and so again must not grasp marks. What is said here should not be taken as mere explanation of section headings. The wondrous purport of prajñā is already entirely contained herein. Just now the distinction was drawn between “leaving” and “not attaching,” whose intent is different. You should further know that though the intent differs, the purport is the same. What is the same? It is cutting off thought. Why? The two sections above on leaving names and words are about leaving the climbing mind — their meaning was already explained at length; leaving conceptual activity is the means of cutting off thought. These two sections on objects and body — that is, dependent and principal rewards — being in every case not to be grasped mean that grasping again gives rise to thought. Though not destroyed, yet not grasped: this too is the means of cutting off thought. There are many other essential meanings; I will explain them layer by layer as they come.

The prajñā-pāramitā of the section above is one of the six pāramitās, and so is a name within the Buddhadharma; yet it is also a name for the principle-and-wisdom inherent in nature. The essence of nature is void and still, and names and words are originally not established in it. Since the section above expounds on the basis of this principle-and-wisdom inherent in nature, it must dispense with all marks. Hence it says only “is not,” says “nothing can be spoken of,” and does not say “is called.” For returning to nature is not being marks, and nature originally has nothing to do with marks; hence it speaks of leaving. The two sections below, on objects and body — which are dependent and principal rewards, with illusory marks plainly there — expound on that basis, and so it is convenient to make plain the meaning of not destroying provisional names. Hence of atoms, worlds, and the thirty-two marks it says “is called.” Yet after all they are illusory marks, delusive and unreal, so it says “is not” and that one should not be attached.

This question likewise follows on the text above. One who grasps marks, hearing that nothing is taught, will say: if nothing is taught, how is the great trichiliocosm taught and transformed? And words are originally without marks, so one may allow that teaching is teaching nothing; but the greatness of a world — its marks are plainly there. How can one say a world is no world? To block this doubt the Buddha asked this question. The question is very subtle: he does not ask about the world, but asks whether all the atoms are many. The meaning is that a world is a gathering of many atoms, which manifests the illusory marks of a great trichiliocosm. One who clings to the marks of the great trichiliocosm as truly existent may thereby suddenly awaken. The answer is subtle too: the elder deeply understood the Buddha’s intent, and so answered “very many,” meaning that all there is in a world is nothing but many atoms. Then apart from the many atoms, is there a separate world? Grasping that there are only many atoms, one knows that the great trichiliocosm exists yet is nonexistent.
(Mao) Next, the direct revelation. This has two parts: (Chen) first, not grasping subtle marks; next, not grasping vast marks.
(Chen) First, not grasping subtle marks.
“Subhūti, the Tathāgata says that all atoms are not atoms; therefore they are called atoms.”

This meaning goes further than the question before. It says that not only is the world not the world, but atoms are not atoms. This makes clear that “atom” too is a provisional name. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “You observe the nature of earth: coarse, it is the great earth; fine, it is an atom, down to the nearest-to-void atom.” What is an atom? What is the nearest-to-void atom? As the Abhidharmakośa and the Nyāyānusāra state, the size of an atom is already the finest thing the eye can see. For seven atoms make one metal-atom, and seven metal-atoms make one water-atom. “Metal-atom” and “water-atom” mean that they can travel through the gaps of metals or the gaps of water — so one may imagine the fineness of an atom. Seven water-atoms make one hare’s-hair atom, said to be as fine as the tip of a hare’s hair; from this one may grasp how fine an atom is. Yet this extremely fine atom can still be analyzed into seven ultimate atoms, which the fleshly eye cannot see; only the divine eye and above can perceive them. This is already the limit of form-marks, and cannot be further analyzed. Yet if observed with the wisdom eye it can be analyzed further into the nearest-to-void atom; “nearest-to-void” means that it is adjacent to empty space. The phrase is like our present saying “equal to zero.” From this one knows that an atom too is a gathering of seven ultimate atoms and is not a real thing. Hence “atoms are not atoms.” This way of speaking is the Small Vehicle’s analysis-of-emptiness contemplation, which requires analyzing one by one before one knows they are empty. The Great Vehicle is otherwise: observing solely in terms of the essence of nature, one knows that no matter whether marks are great or small, all are produced by conditions, illusorily existent, and empty right where they are; what need is there to analyze before knowing? To contemplate thus is named the contemplation of the emptiness of essence. This sutra is spoken for those who have aroused the Great Vehicle and the supreme vehicle; hence it says “the Tathāgata says.” “Tathāgata” is a name for the virtue of nature; “the Tathāgata says” makes clear that the observation is made in reliance on the original emptiness of the essence of nature — the so-called contemplation of the emptiness of essence. For spoken in terms of nature, atoms are originally without real substance, yet are not without illusory marks. Being originally without real substance, it says “is not”; not being without illusory marks, it says “is called.”
(Chen) Next, not grasping vast marks.
“The Tathāgata says that the world is not the world; therefore it is called the world.”

Knowing that atoms are not atoms but merely provisional names, one understands without further words that the world is not the world but merely a provisional name. Such is the skillfulness of this way of speaking. Taking these two small sections together, the intent is that one who cultivates prajñā, whatever the object — a matter as fine as an atom or as great as a world — should neither destroy nor grasp it. If even what is as fine as an atom should not be destroyed, how much less what is greater; if even what is as great as a world should not be grasped, how much less what is finer.
(Yin) Next, revealing that one should uphold it while not grasping bodily marks.

“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?” “No, World-Honored One. Why? What the Tathāgata calls the thirty-two marks are not marks; therefore they are called the thirty-two marks.”

This question likewise arises from the text above. One who does not grasp the intent, hearing that the world is not the world but a provisional name, will say: the Buddha, responding to each occasion, manifests various bodies precisely to teach and transform the living beings of the great trichiliocosm. If, as said above, the world exists yet is nonexistent and is nonexistent yet exists, then why does the Buddha manifest the response body of the thirty-two marks? Is the response body too existent yet nonexistent, nonexistent yet existent? To block this doubt the Buddha asked this question. You should know that the Tathāgata, having already realized nature, nonetheless manifests the body of the thirty-two marks because living beings each have this tathāgatagarbha as their substance, yet pitifully are deluded by marks and do not know it themselves. Hence from the essence of nature he manifests the marks of the response body to teach and transform the great trichiliocosm, opening this treasury for living beings, causing them all to turn the light back and shine within, not grasp any marks, and see the original nature for themselves. This nature of living beings is originally one substance with all Buddhas — what is called the one true dharma-realm. Hence if one can see the original nature for oneself, one sees the Tathāgata. If one grasps marks, what one sees is the marks of the response body, not the essence of the dharmakāya; how can that be called seeing the Tathāgata? Understanding how the Tathāgata should be seen, one knows that the thirty-two marks too are produced by the meeting of conditions and are empty right where they are. Empty right where they are, they exist yet are nonexistent; produced by the meeting of conditions, they are nonexistent yet existent. Existing yet nonexistent, it says “are not marks”; nonexistent yet existent, it says “are called the thirty-two marks.”

The wording of the question here has the same tone as “can the Tathāgata be seen by bodily marks?” in the first great section, but the meaning is not entirely the same. There the question was raised in terms of bodily marks, including both the Buddha and living beings; here the question is raised in terms of the thirty-two marks, and refers specifically to the Buddha.

The answer “no” is a living phrase, with the same meaning as the “no” in the earlier answer about whether the Tathāgata can be seen by bodily marks: it says one cannot see him by them, and also that one can see him by them. The current circulating editions add, after “no,” the sentence “the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks.” The ancient text lacks it, and rightly so. You should know that in the section above the text below says only that bodily marks are not bodily marks, and so says “cannot,” and also says that the Tathāgata is seen by bodily marks — making clear that the “no” above and the “bodily marks are not bodily marks” below are both living phrases with double meaning. And here the text below already says “are not marks” and “are called the thirty-two marks,” which is quite enough to show that the “no” carries a double meaning. What need is there to add yet another sentence, “the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks”? One should follow the ancient text.

It says “the Tathāgata says” to make clear that this is spoken in terms of nature. Spoken in terms of nature, they are not marks: this makes clear that the essence of nature is originally not marks. If one knows that the essence is not marks, how can the thirty-two marks see the Tathāgata? Now it says that spoken in terms of nature they are not marks, and are called the thirty-two marks: this makes clear that a name is the guest of the reality. Since the thirty-two marks are merely a name, one may understand that their essence is nature. If one knows this principle and can be unattached to marks, then through the marks one can realize the essence — why must one annihilate the marks to see nature? Knowing this, one also clearly understands that the thirty-two marks originally arise from nature and so should not be destroyed, while nature is originally not marks and so should not be grasped.
What a great trichiliocosm is has already been discussed at length. As for what the thirty-two marks are, their meaning must likewise not go unknown.
(1) The mark of level and even feet: the soles of the feet have no hollows but are entirely full and level.
(2) The mark of the thousand-spoked wheel: the pattern beneath the feet is round like a wheel, and within the wheel are a thousand spokes, signifying that all marks are complete.
(3) The mark of long, slender fingers: the fingers are straight and tapered, fine, round, and long.
(4) The mark of soft and supple hands and feet: both hands and feet are as soft as cotton.
(5) The mark of webbed hands and feet: the fingers and toes are as if joined by a net, linked and interlaced with one another, like the shape between the toes of geese and ducks.
(6) The mark of full and complete heels: the heel is fully rounded, without hollows.
(7) The mark of high and beautiful insteps: the instep is high, arched, and full.

(8) The mark of calves like those of the king of deer: the calves are even and full, unlike the calves of ordinary people, which suddenly thicken. (The Chinese character for “calf” is here given two fanqie readings, one as in “Shan,” one as in “chuan”; in antiquity the calf was also called fei, pronounced “fei.”)
(9) The mark of hands reaching past the knees: when both arms hang down, their length passes the knees.
(10) The mark of the horse’s concealed organ: the male organ is closely concealed and not exposed.
(11) The mark of the body’s height and breadth being equal: from head to foot, the height equals the span of the outstretched arms.
(12) The mark of blue hairs growing from the pores: from each pore grows a single blue hair, without disorder.
(13) The mark of the body hair curling upward: every hair on the body curls to the right with its tip pointing up.
(14) The mark of a golden body: the body’s color is like a gathering of purple-gold light.
(15) The mark of constant light extending one zhang: the body emits radiance, one zhang in each of the four directions.
(16) The mark of fine, smooth skin: the skin is delicate and lustrous, neither holding dust or water nor letting mosquitoes and gnats alight.

(17) The mark of seven places full and level: the soles of both feet, both palms, both shoulders (that is, the hollows of the shoulders), and the nape of the neck — these seven places are all full and level, without the least defect.
